`_needs_fix_task` returns `True` for a bug whose `fix_task` is a finished task it was not declared to fix, **except** when the finished task is `ABANDONED` and the bug id happens to be in that task's `fixes`. The `state in (DONE, ABANDONED) and b.id not in fixes_of(...)` clause groups `ABANDONED` with `DONE`, but the justification given in the comment ("A done task's OWN bug is not refiled: `verify --reopen` sends that task back") only holds for `DONE`; an abandoned task will never be sent back by `verify --reopen`, so nothing will ever fix the bug.

Concrete failure: `bug found --item T --same-fix` for a report against another bug's open fix task `T` adds the report's id `B` to `T.fixes` (the "same fix" path the intent explicitly describes). If `T` is later abandoned, then in `bug_file_tasks` we get `_live(st, T) == True`, `T.state == ABANDONED`, and `B in fixes_of(st, T)`, so `_needs_fix_task` returns `False`. `B` is left in `st.bugs` with `open=True` and `fix_task="T"`, it is excluded from `todo`, and `bug file-tasks` never files `fix-B` — exactly the "open bug pointing at a finished task" orphan (`B8dcbf2f8da`) that this change is supposed to repair, only reachable via the abandoned branch rather than the done branch. The exemption for `fixes_of` must be limited to `DONE` (e.g. return `True` unconditionally when the live task is `ABANDONED`).

chunk_findings.detail: The `b.id not in fixes_of(st, b.fix_task)` gate is applied to *both* `DONE` and `ABANDONED`, but it is only sound for `DONE`. `fixes_of` reports the bugs a task declares it fixes (that is how `complete` decides which bugs to close, per the B7bdcc6b212 change noted in the intent), and that set is state-independent: an abandoned `fix-<bug>` task still lists `bug` in its fixes. So a bug whose *own* fix task was abandoned is judged "already fixed" and never refiled, even though an abandoned task by definition did not fix it — the exact orphan class this change exists to repair. Concrete repro: `bug found` creates open bug B and `fix-B` (with `fix-B.fixes = {B}`, `B.fix_task = fix-B`); run `ddflow abandon fix-B` (fix-B now `ABANDONED`, B still open); run `ddflow bug file-tasks`. For B, `_live(st, 'fix-B')` is True, the state is `ABANDONED`, and `b.id in fixes_of(st, 'fix-B')`, so `_needs_fix_task` returns False and B is excluded from `todo`; B stays open pointing at a dead task forever. The comment above the return only justifies the exemption for `DONE` ("verify --reopen sends that task back"); no such mechanism covers `ABANDONED`, so the condition should refile when the fix task is `ABANDONED` (or only exempt `DONE` tasks that actually list the bug).

chunk_findings.detail: `seed()` builds the "legacy" state it needs — a report whose `fix_task` is *another* bug's fix task — by calling the very API the change alters: `K.bug_found(repo, summary="kill-wait test flakes", item="fix-Bx", id="Brep", agent="a")`. The stated intent of this change is that `bug found` must now "file fix-<bug> for a report against another bug's fix task (or add it to the task's fixes when the reporter says it is the same fix)". `fix-Bx` is exactly another bug's (Bx's) fix task, and the seed passes no "same fix" declaration, so on the fixed code this call files `fix-Brep` and sets `Brep.fix_task == "fix-Brep"`. The line immediately after it, `assert state(repo).bugs["Brep"].fix_task == "fix-Bx"`, therefore fails, and every test in the file fails inside `seed()` — the regression suite can never go green on the fixed code (and if part 1 does *not* change `bug_found`, then the behavior the intent promises is simply missing). The pre-fix state has to be constructed from the raw log events (`bug.found` for `Brep` with `fix_task`/item `fix-Bx`) rather than by invoking the changed API, or the call must explicitly request the "same fix" outcome that the new code only produces on request.

chunk_findings.detail: The new branch makes `_needs_fix_task` return `False` for *any* open bug whose `fix_task` is an abandoned task named `fix-<bug>`, regardless of whether that task ever fixed the bug. The stated goal of this change is to "refile an open bug whose fix_task is done/abandoned without fixing it", and an abandoned own task is precisely that case, yet `bug file-tasks` will now never refile it. Concrete input: a bug `Brep` whose `fix_task` is `fix-Brep` (its own task) is abandoned, e.g. `item.abandoned fix-Brep`; running `bug file-tasks` calls `_needs_fix_task(Brep)`, reaches `return b.fix_task != FIX_TASK_PREFIX + b.id`, and since `"fix-Brep" == FIX_TASK_PREFIX + "Brep"` it returns `False`, so no task is filed and nothing is linked. `Brep` is left open pointing at a task that will never run — the same "orphaned report pointing at a dead task" failure the change is meant to eliminate, just for the bug's own task instead of a task it was reported against. The docstring's justification ("a refile could only link again") is not demonstrated by the change either: the only linking shown (test 1) is to a task that already lists the bug in `fixes`, whereas the abandoned case here is short-circuited before any link target is chosen. To be consistent with the stated behaviour, either the abandoned own task should still cause a refile (with the link path excluding a dead task), or the carve-out needs a concrete mechanism ensuring the bug still gets fixed before `False` is returned.

chunk_findings.detail: The "Next" block is computed asymmetrically. The ready branch maps each plan entry to its id: `ready = [it.id for it in plan.ready[:NEXT_SHOWN]]`. The capped branch does not: `lines.append(f"Next (when a slot frees): {', '.join(plan.capped[:NEXT_SHOWN])}")`. If `plan.ready`/`plan.capped` are sequences of the same element type (both are item objects — which the `.id` in the ready branch implies), then `', '.join(...)` on the capped slice raises `TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, <Item> found`. The trigger is exactly the scenario the branch exists for: `plan.ready` is empty while `plan.capped` is non-empty (ready work exists but is held back by the parallelism cap). Then `report()` crashes instead of emitting `Next (when a slot frees): ...`, so the progress report never renders for a saturated queue. The fix is to map to ids as in the ready branch (`', '.join(it.id for it in plan.capped[:NEXT_SHOWN])`). If `plan.capped` is in fact a list of ids while `plan.ready` is a list of items, this is fine — but that asymmetry would be surprising given the two attributes describe the same set of schedulable items.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite drops the falsy guard that the previous version carried: `bool(git_ref) and (...)`. The old expression short-circuited on a falsy `git_ref`, so a job whose ref field was `null` simply did not cover the commit and returned `False`. The new body unconditionally executes `git_ref.rsplit("..", 1)` as its first statement, so the same input now raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'rsplit'`. The original `bool(git_ref)` guard is itself evidence that roborev job records can carry a missing/`null` ref (otherwise the guard would be dead code for the empty-string case it already handles correctly). Concretely: `roborev list --json` returns a job entry with `"ref": null`; a caller forwarding that value (`_covers(job.get("ref"), sha)`) previously got `False` ("no finished review of this commit"), and now the whole `review_of` call — and therefore the standards gate that depends on it — blows up instead of reporting an unchecked/missing review. In the old code, any falsy `note` (the same falsy-ness the `X or Y` idiom was written to tolerate) still yielded a diagnostic such as `"roborev job ? names no agent"`. Now, if `RR.review_of` returns `(None, None)` — e.g. no roborev review/roborev output could be located for the reviewed SHA — `why` becomes `None`, so `ev["roborev"]` is recorded as `{"verified": False, "why": None}` and the caller returns `f"NOTE: {why}."` = `"NOTE: None."`. Demonstrable input: any task whose `reviewed_sha` has no matching roborev job and for which `review_of` supplies no note. Downstream consumers that treat the evidence `why` as a string (formatting, `.lower()`, persistence/schema expectations) now see `null`/`"None."` instead of the previous human-readable reason. The `or` in the removed line existed precisely to guarantee a message here, and that guarantee is no longer met.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff is presented as the fix for B03437a6b45 ("standards gate trusts the requested roborev agent, not the one that ran"), but the only behavioral change it makes is to the error-message fallback in the *no-answer* path. Nothing in the changed hunk compares the reviewer roborev actually used (`rv.agent` / `rv.model`) against the typed model, and nothing changes the fact that once `rv.reviewer` is truthy the branch unconditionally sets `verified: True` and returns `typed`. Concretely: enqueue a review with `--model kilo`, let roborev run it on `claude-code`, so `review_of` returns `rv.agent == "claude-code"`, `rv.model == "claude-code"`, `rv.reviewer` truthy. `rv is None or not rv.reviewer` is False, so the code falls through to `ev["roborev"] = {"verified": True, "job": rv.job, "agent": rv.agent, "model": rv.model}` and credits `typed` ("kilo"). The mismatch is still accepted as verified evidence for kilo — exactly the bug the intent describes. The added regression test (`test_an_unanswered_lookup_still_records_a_reason`) stubs `review_of` to return `(None, "")`, i.e. it exercises only the `rv is None` message path; it would pass identically even if the gate still trusted the requested agent, so it does not guard the reported bug. If the real mismatch check lives in an unseen caller this is a non-issue, but as delivered the change does not touch the trust decision its intent claims to fix.
